question: A 32-year-old woman weighs 62 kg and is 158 cm tall. Using the India-specific BMI cut-offs, how would you classify her nutritional status?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Her BMI is approximately 24.8 kg/m², which exceeds the Indian normal upper limit of 22.9 kg/m². Using standard WHO cut-offs she would be classified as normal, but India uses lower thresholds due to higher cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI.

Correct. Her BMI is ~24.8 kg/m². India-specific cut-offs (endorsed by ICMR) classify ≥23 kg/m² as overweight and ≥25 kg/m² as obese, reflecting increased cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI in South Asians.
Obesity Class I by Indian cut-offs begins at ≥25 kg/m². Her BMI of ~24.8 kg/m² falls just below this threshold, placing her in the overweight category.
Her BMI of ~24.8 kg/m² is well above the underweight threshold of <18.5 kg/m².

overallFeedback.feedback: Calculate BMI as weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²) = 62 ÷ (1.58)² ≈ 24.8 kg/m². Using Indian cut-offs, ≥23 kg/m² = overweight and ≥25 kg/m² = obese.
Excellent. Applying India-specific BMI cut-offs is essential — South Asians develop metabolic complications at lower BMI than Western populations.
